Question: for one program in one year, the budget report, the financial statements, the bank and the performance report show different amounts. Which amount measures what, and why do correct records differ? Idea: one purchase passes five moments on different dates: authority is given, a commitment is made, a delivery is accepted, cash is paid, and a result is counted. Each moment has its own record and its own report. The totals of a year differ because the moments occur in different periods. The difference is not an error. It is information: it shows what is committed but not delivered, delivered but not paid, or paid but not used. How to read it: each row is one measure, in the order of time. Column 2 = the record in which the event is first written. Column 3 = the report that adds the records. Column 4 (grey) = what explains the difference between this measure and the measure in the next row. Column 5 (violet) = a check that connects two measures. When the comparison works: two amounts may be compared when they have the same measure, the same period and the same coverage of funds. Example: obligations in FAR 1 of two agencies for the same year. When it fails: an obligation rate of 95 percent does not show that 95 percent of the goods were delivered or paid. Row B measures commitments, not deliveries or payments. Sources: registries and the reports FAR 1, FAR 1-A, FAR 1-C, FAR 3, FAR 4 and BAR 1 [JC2019-1] . Which record is written at which event, and the journal entry at the accepted delivery [GAM-V1 Annex H, Ch.3 ss.8-17] . Part C of the obligation request shows obligation, payable and payment of one obligation [GAM-V2 App.11] . The statement of comparison of budget and actual amounts, and the three kinds of difference that it must explain [GAM-V1 Ch.3 ss.25-30] . Bank reconciliation each month [GAM-V1 Ch.21 s.4] . Financial statements and their submission [PD1445 s.41] [COA-GAS] . Physical plan (BED 2), cash operations report of BTr, lapse of the NCA, transfers not disbursed until used [NBC599] . The financial result in the bonus rules is cash disbursements measured against the NCA received [PBB2024] . Bank reconciliation: "most active government accounts are reconciled quarterly" (indicator 27.1, score C); unliquidated advances (indicator 27.3, score C) [PEFA2025] . In BTMS the registries, the books and the reports come from one set of records [CL2025-8] . A difference between rule and reported practice: the Manual requires a bank reconciliation statement each month [GAM-V1 Ch.21 s.4] . The assessment of 2025 reports that most active accounts are reconciled each quarter [PEFA2025] .

Question: for each event of one purchase, which unit of the agency and which other body writes a record, what does each record say, and where does one body record nothing although another body has recorded the event? Idea: no single record contains the whole transaction. Five units or bodies write about the same money, each in its own record and on its own date. An obligation exists only in the registries of the budget unit. The first journal entry of the purchase itself is made when the delivery is accepted. The Treasury records the spending of the agency only when the bank has paid. A cell with the words "No record" is therefore information: it shows which body cannot see the event from its own records. How to read it: each row is one event, in the order of time. Each column is one keeper of records. Column 1 = the event. Column 2 (blue) = budget unit of the agency: registries, no double entry. Column 3 (green) = accounting unit of the agency: books with double entry. Column 4 (white) = cash unit and property unit of the agency. Column 5 (orange) = the servicing bank. Column 6 (yellow) = books of the national government kept by BTr. Column 7 (violet) = books of BIR. Grey with a dashed border = this keeper writes nothing at this event. The diagram has no arrows: the cells of one row are records of the same event, and they are not steps that follow one another. When the records agree: at the end of a month the cash account of the agency for its NCA equals the balance of the NCA in the bank statement, after the items in transit are listed. The monthly bank reconciliation statement shows this [GAM-V1 Ch.21] . When they disagree without an error: a payment order is issued on the last day of the month. The agency has credited its cash account (row 5). The bank and the Treasury have recorded nothing yet (row 6). The three records differ by this amount until the bank pays. Sources: which record is written at which event, and that appropriation, allotment and obligation have no journal entry [GAM-V1 Annex H, Ch.3 ss.8-17] . Part C of the obligation request with the columns obligation, payable and payment [GAM-V2 App.11] . Tax Remittance Advice in three sets of books [GAM-V1 Ch.5 s.38, Annex H] . Reversion of the unused NCA [GAM-V1 Ch.19 s.55] . The reconciliations of row 9 [GAM-V1 Ch.2 s.8, Ch.21 s.4] . The cells that say no entry in the example: the worked example of the Manual lists the entries of the Treasury. It contains no entry of the Treasury for the issue of an NCA and none for a lapsed NCA [GAM-V1 Annex H] . I did not read the accounting rules of BTr itself. Same-day deposit of collections with authorized government depository banks, investment of idle balances, Bond Sinking Fund [EO449] . Daily transfer of collections, some foreign-funded and trust accounts outside the TSA [PEFA2025] . Shares of local governments released directly by BTr through servicing banks [GAA2026-GP] . t: Diagram 15b: Transfer of funds from one agency to another body that will implement

Question: an agency gives its money to another agency, a corporation or a local government to implement a project. When is the money "spent", and who is responsible for it? Idea: a transfer moves cash but not accountability. Under the FY 2026 rules the source agency may not treat the transfer as a disbursement until the receiver has used it for works, goods or services that were delivered, inspected and accepted. Until then the source agency holds a receivable and the receiver holds a liability. Sources: transfers to other agencies, corporations and local governments are not treated as disbursed by the source until used by the receiver for accepted deliveries within the validity period [NBC599 s.3.4] . A part of the advances, in particular advances to government corporations, was not liquidated at the end of 2023 (indicator 27.3, score C) [PEFA2025] . Schedule of fund transfers required from corporations [COA2015-004] . From the accounting manual of 2015: the memorandum of agreement, the amount (enough for three months, or the total project cost), the check in the name of the implementing agency for its trust account, its official receipt, the monthly reports within ten days, the return of an unused balance when the agreement says so, the audit by the auditor of the implementing agency [GAM-V1 Ch.6 s.63] . The entries of both agencies side by side: Due from National Government Agencies in the books of the source, Due to NGAs in the trust fund books of the implementer [GAM-V1 Annex M] . A condition in the manual: the receivable and the liability are recorded when the agreement requires that unused money is returned. When the agreement has no such condition, the source agency records an expense and the receiver records revenue at the transfer [GAM-V1 Ch.6 s.63] . The diagram shows the first case. t: Diagram 15e: Money for disasters: standby funds of agencies, the national fund, and the fund of each local government

Question: after a disaster, money is needed within days, and the normal path (release request, procurement, payment) takes months. Which money is already available, who must approve the rest, and which records show the use? Idea: speed is obtained in three ways. First, an amount is placed in advance in the budgets of the agencies that respond first (Quick Response Fund), so that no release is needed at the moment of the disaster. Second, a national fund without a named project is kept in the budget law and released case by case. Third, every local government must set aside its own fund each year. t: Diagram 17d: Why UACS alone cannot follow one contract: a code names a class, a document number names one record
x: Question: is UACS the key that connects all PFM records? For which questions is it enough, and for which is it not? Question: is UACS the key that connects all PFM records? For which questions is it enough, and for which is it not? Idea: a UACS code names a group of records: all records with the same funding source, office, area, purpose and object. It does not name one record inside the group. Two contracts paid from the same budget line have exactly the same UACS code on every record. To separate them you need the numbers of the documents. Example (invented, for illustration only): one budget line funds two contracts. Every box in the same colour has the same UACS code. The records of contract A and of contract B differ only in their document numbers. A question that UACS answers: how much was allotted, obligated and paid under this program, by this office, for this expense class, in this year? All records with the same code are summed. This is what report FAR 1 does. A question that UACS does not answer: which payments belong to contract B, and was the work of contract B accepted before each payment? The code is the same for A and B. The answer needs the chain ORS number, voucher number, payment order number, and the contract number, which is not a coded field on the obligation request. Sources: UACS is a classification with segments for funding source, organization, location, program and object [JC2017-1] . The location code is the area of mandate of the operating unit, not the site of a project [JC2017-1 s.5.2] . Fields of the obligation request and of the payment order [GAM-V2 App.11, App.42] . NCA number on payment orders that agencies published [LDDAP-FORM] . FAR 1 by program and by object [JC2019-1] . Record links stored by the system in BTMS [BTMS-SITE] .

Question: the budget law contains targets in units (for example classrooms built), not only amounts in pesos. Where is a target written, who reports the result, who checks the report, and who uses it? Idea: performance information has its own line of records, parallel to the line of money. The target is fixed with the appropriation. The result is reported by the agency itself each quarter. DBM reviews the results each year. Three other users take the same reports for other purposes: the bonus system, the public portal, and the evaluators and auditors. How to read it: the row from left to right is the main path through one year. The column after the quarterly report shows the five uses of the reported results. Three of them lead to the next budget. Blue = executive. Purple = Congress. Green = spending agency. Light orange = audit. Dotted arrows = information. When the path works: a target that is a count of things delivered by the agency itself (for example kilometres of road completed) can be reported and checked against contracts and acceptance reports. When it fails: a target that depends on other actors (for example the rate of school completion) can be reported, but the report does not show whether the spending caused the result. That question needs an evaluation (see 18b). Sources: program structure with outcome and output indicators in the budget proposal [NBM156] . Physical plan (BED 2) [NBC599] . Quarterly Physical Report of Operations (BAR 1) through URS within 30 days after each quarter [JC2019-1] . Agency Performance Review, and the four criteria of the bonus: performance results against the targets approved by Congress, process results, financial results (cash disbursements against the NCA received), citizen satisfaction, 25 points each [PBB2024] . Suspension of the earlier performance management and incentive systems for review [EO61] . National Evaluation Policy Framework of 2015, revised in 2025, with a steering committee [NEPF] [NEPF-NEWS] . COMPASS portal: program and project performance, financial performance and implementation status for the public [EO126] . Monitoring of selected projects with digital images [ROADMAP-MID] . t: Diagram 19a: Fiscal risks: payments that the Treasury may have to make, although no budget line of today names them
x: Question: the budget law lists the spending that is decided. Which possible payments are not decided, where could they come from, who monitors each source, and from which authority would a payment be made if the event occurs? Question: the budget law lists the spending that is decided. Which possible payments are not decided, where could they come from, who monitors each source, and from which authority would a payment be made if the event occurs? Idea: a fiscal risk is an event that would change revenue, spending or debt compared with the plan. One group of risks are contingent liabilities: the government has promised to pay IF a stated event occurs (for example, if a corporation cannot repay a guaranteed loan). Such a promise costs nothing on the day it is made, so it does not appear as spending. It appears only in a risk statement, until the event occurs. How to read it: each row is one source of risk, in the order of the chapters of the Fiscal Risks Statement. Column 2 = the office that monitors it. Column 3 (grey) = the authority from which a payment would be made if the event occurs. Sources: the Fiscal Risks Statement is issued by the DBCC. Its chapters cover macroeconomic assumptions, fiscal performance, public debt, the financial sector, and "Other Contingent Central Government Obligations": government corporations, public-private partnerships and other contingent liabilities, local governments, natural disasters [FRS2023] . Members of the DBCC [DBCC-PAGE] [AO37] . Interest and net lending as automatic appropriations, budgetary support to corporations, the Contingent Fund and the disaster fund as items released by SARO [NBC599] . The PPP Risk Management Fund pays contingent liabilities from partnerships; the PPP Center manages it and the DBCC sets its target amount [RA11966 s.27] . Disaster funds, see 15e [GAA2026-NDRRMF] . BLGF certifies the borrowing capacity of local governments [DOF-LGULOAN] . Rows of the consolidated public sector position [BESF2026-A3] . In the accounts and in the law: a contingent liability is disclosed in the notes and is not recorded as a liability [GAM-V1 Ch.18 s.3] . A guarantee of the national government that is called is paid from an automatic appropriation, and corporations report their guaranteed obligations to DOF and DBM [EO292-B6 s.26, s.30] . An asset built by a private operator under a concession is recorded by the government body that granted it, with a liability of the same amount [GAM-V1 Ch.14 s.3, s.5] . General knowledge, not opened in a source here: that DOF and BTr decide on guarantees for the loans of corporations; that the Governance Commission for GOCCs monitors the performance of corporations; unprogrammed appropriations as a source of payment; the statement in row 5 that no national authority pays the debts of a local government by rule. The latest Fiscal Risks Statement that I could open is that of 2023, and its last chapter was cut in my copy. Not covered by the assessment pages I read: indicator 10 (fiscal risk reporting) of the 2025 assessment [PEFA2025] .

Which bodies approve such a project, and at which points does it enter the budget? Idea: a partnership moves payments into later years and adds promises that depend on events. The controls are therefore placed before the contract is signed: approval by a body above the agency when the cost is high or when money of the budget is promised, and clearance of each promise by the Department of Finance. t: Lesson 3: Authority to commit is not cash

An appropriation is not an obligation, an allotment is not a bank balance, and a Notice of Cash Allocation is not itself a transfer of cash. Different permissions, different records An appropriation provides legal spending authority under specified terms. The applicable allotment mechanism permits the agency to incur obligations. A valid obligation records a commitment. Cash authority subsequently limits permitted disbursement under the relevant banking arrangement. The atlas distinguishes GAA-as-allotment-order from SARO or GARO cases and other special arrangements. These vary by fiscal year and classification: consult Chapter 05 rather than applying one release instrument universally. Control check: Neither a release document nor a UACS code proves that a particular supplier received money. The payment and settlement records are separate evidence. Before the government pays, somebody must establish why a particular amount is owed to a particular party—and whether all statutory and documentary conditions are satisfied. The standard contract-payment path Procurement planning leads to bidding, evaluation and award where applicable. The certificate of funds, the obligation and the contract follow, then delivery, inspection and acceptance, and the examination of the claim. t: Reference H — PFM system model: typed events, records, authorities, jurisdictions
x: Historical research reference (10 October 2026). Proposed modeling material, not the current procedural atlas and not an official information-system specification. Some older diagram IDs and claims have been superseded. Reference H — PFM system model: typed events, records, authorities, jurisdictions Status: proposed reference ontology; not enacted law, not BTMS database schema. This document strengthens the descriptive atlas without claiming the public PFM applications share one internal implementation. 1. Ontological layers Jurisdiction and financial entity: NGA, attached operating unit, LGU, GOCC, GFI, BARMM and special statutory funds can have different spending powers and reporting boundaries. An entity is not an application account. Authority: a law, appropriation item, allotment instrument, signed approval or delegated competence. Authorities have author, recipient, amount/purpose limits and validity intervals; authority is not cash. Event: a dated occurrence or state change (assessment, appropriation enactment, allotment, obligation, delivery, payment, journal posting, reconciliation, audit notice). Events may be planned, recorded, reversed or corrected. Event records must carry IDs and provenance. Record: one identifiable, versioned document, register line, contract, transaction or journal entry. A record's issuer differs from the software displaying a copy. Classification: UACS (with funding, organization, location, program/PAP, object dimensions as applicable), COA accounts and other code systems. Classification codes are types , not unique document or event identifiers. Financial or physical state: allotment balance, unpaid obligations, payables, bank cash, asset ownership, delivered output or claim status. These are not automatically equal amounts. System and interface: named application and deployment scope, data owner, exchange method, evidence, and reconciliation; a system in a slide is not evidence of an implemented integration. 2. Explicit predicates and relationships AUTHORIZES(authority,event,rule_version) ; EVIDENCES(record,event) ; REFERENCES(record_1,record_2,role) ; CLASSIFIES(record,code,version,valid_at) ; RECORDED_IN(record,system,environment) ; SENT_VIA(exchange,source_system,target_system,mode) ; CHANGES(event,balance,amount,as_of) ; CONSTRains(rule,event,period) ; SUPERSEDES(new_record,old_record) ; RECONCILES(record_a,record_b,as_of) . References are explicitly many-to-many. One contract can have several obligations, releases and payments; one UACS class can cover many unrelated payments. Shared coding never proves shared identity. An interface may preserve one ID, map it to another, or lose it, and this difference must be recorded. 3. Time is mandatory Store at least event_date , posting_date , fiscal_year , authority_valid_from/to , code_version/effective_date , and evidence_checked_at . A document dated 2025 might pay under 2026 rules; the transaction must be assessed under the appropriate law and fund validity. Cross-year comparison needs a documented code crosswalk, not silent recoding. 4. Modeling conventions observed : authoritative primary documents or operational evidence examined. reported : credible publication says practice exists; no independently tested interface. inferred : model joins established facts but technical or legal conditionality remains unverified. target : planned architecture, never a production assertion. unknown : absence of evidence; never assert an integration does not exist. Reference diagrams: 00i , 00k , 17e , 17g . Primary research anchors: DBM PFM Roadmap Midterm Update ; COA Government Accounting Manual; FY 2026 NBC 599 . The ontology itself is this atlas's proposed analytic structure. ← Research models

t: Reference I — IFMIS and interface evidence protocol
x: Historical research reference (10 October 2026). Proposed modeling material, not the current procedural atlas and not an official information-system specification. Some older diagram IDs and claims have been superseded. Reference I — IFMIS and interface evidence protocol 1. The minimum assertion Do not write A → B (API) merely because both applications are mentioned in an integration roadmap. An assertion about integration must state source and destination application , specific owner and deployment context , type of payload , transmission mechanism , operational status , date , and evidence level . The original interface register is preserved verbatim. The interface evidence register re-expresses each legacy row as a claim requiring validation ; its blank mechanism, deployment and protocol fields are intentional, not signs of failure. It does not assert that blank fields mean an interface is absent. 2. Orthogonal evidence axes Dimension Controlled vocabulary Meaning Deployment production_confirmed , pilot_reported , planned , retired , unknown Whether operational rollout has been proved for the specified agency/scope Mechanism api , batch , file_import , web_portal , manual_reentry , paper , bank_network , unknown How a record moves Evidence primary_operational , official_policy , official_announcement , secondary_report , atlas_inference , unverified Why the model makes a claim Authoritative data source_record , copy , transform , unknown Which is the record of authority Reconciliation automated , manual , none_verified , unknown How cross-system equality is checked An agency can be in a BTMS rollout without every companion system operating an API. Official DBM FY 2026 statement says BTMS piloted in seven agencies in 2025, intended expansion to 155 in 2026. The midterm roadmap schedules longer implementation of integration, migration and UACS revision. These official statements are evidence of program rollout/plan , not successful agency-by-agency data exchange. 3. Proof hierarchy and negative claims A current production log, agency acceptance record, bank confirmation, or system transaction record with a specified scope proves an operational interface for that scope and date. A current approved system manual or integration specification supports a design; it may not prove operation. An official roadmap proves an intention or implementation work plan; it does not prove completed deployment. Two systems named in a common diagram do not prove an electronic interface. A reusable classification code does not prove shared database keys. An absent public source is not proof that an exchange is impossible. Mark unknown unless there is explicit verified negative evidence. 4. Interface failure contract Every confirmed or proposed interface needs identifier translation, immutable source references, idempotency/duplicate detection, cutoff and retry policy, reconciliation ownership, exception queue, and data dictionary versioning. Treat these as recommended technical requirements unless an actual legal or technical document mandates them. Diagrams: 16h , 16i , 16j . ← Research models
